title: Matter and changes
intro: Matter has mass and occupies space. Composition distinguishes pure substances (elements and compounds) from mixtures; physical state distinguishes solids, liquids, gases and plasmas.
detail: A physical change alters form or state while preserving chemical identity. A chemical change produces substances with different compositions or bonding. Mixtures can have variable proportions; a pure compound has a defined composition. Changes of colour, heat or gas are clues, but the whole observation and possible alternatives must be examined.
example: Melting ice is physical because both ice and liquid water are H₂O. Burning wood is chemical because new substances form. Salt water is a mixture: removing water can separate its components without changing the salt into another substance.
question: Which example is a chemical change?
explanation: Combustion forms new compounds, so it is a chemical change.
summary: Classify matter by composition before classifying its change. A visible change alone does not establish a chemical reaction.
objectives: Classify a sample as an element, compound or mixture
Explain the distinction between physical and chemical changes

questions.question: Which example is a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Combustion forms new compounds, so it is a chemical change.

questions.question: How is homogeneous salt water classified?
questions.explanation: Salt water contains more than one substance and its proportions can vary.

questions.question: Why do bubbles alone not prove a reaction?
options: They may be vapour during boiling
Every gas is a new element
questions.explanation: Vaporisation is a physical change; the identities of the substances are needed to interpret the observation.

title: Atoms and particles
intro: An atom contains a nucleus of positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons, surrounded by negatively charged electrons. The nucleus contains nearly all the atomic mass.
detail: Atomic number Z is the proton count and identifies the element. Mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons in one isotope. A neutral atom has Z electrons. Losing electrons makes a positive ion; gaining electrons makes a negative ion without changing the element. Electrons are described by quantum states, not tiny planets on fixed classical paths.
example: For sodium-23, Z=11 and A=23: neutrons = 23−11 = 12. Na⁺ still has 11 protons and 12 neutrons but has 10 electrons.
question: How many neutrons are in sodium-23?
explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23−11.
summary: Protons identify the element; neutrons distinguish isotopes; electron gain or loss produces ions.
objectives: Calculate a neutron count from A and Z
Determine the electron count of a simple ion

questions.question: How many neutrons are in sodium-23?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23−11.

questions.question: How many electrons does Na⁺ have if Z=11?
questions.explanation: A singly positive ion has lost one electron: 11−1=10.

questions.question: Which change changes the element?
questions.explanation: An element is identified by its atomic number, the number of protons.

title: The periodic table and trends
intro: The modern periodic table orders elements by increasing atomic number. Rows are periods and columns are groups. Electron configurations explain many recurring properties.
detail: Atomic radius generally decreases across a main-group period because effective nuclear attraction increases. It generally increases down a group as occupied shells are added. Ionisation energy often follows the opposite pattern. These are trends with exceptions, not absolute rules. Elements in one main group have related valence electron configurations; hydrogen has distinctive behaviour.
example: Sodium and potassium are alkali metals. Potassium generally has the larger atomic radius because its valence electron occupies a higher principal shell. Group 18 contains noble gases; their low reactivity is not a claim that every member forms no compounds.
question: What determines the order in the modern table?
explanation: Elements are ordered by atomic number, their proton count.
summary: Use atomic number for ordering, groups for recurring valence behaviour, and qualified trends for comparing properties.
objectives: Identify groups and periods
Compare radii of elements in one group

questions.question: What determines the order in the modern table?
questions.explanation: Elements are ordered by atomic number, their proton count.

questions.question: What are the columns of the periodic table called?
questions.explanation: Columns are groups and rows are periods.

questions.question: Why is potassium generally larger than sodium?
options: Its valence electron occupies a higher principal shell
questions.explanation: An additional occupied shell increases atomic extent despite the larger proton count.

title: Chemical bonds
intro: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Covalent bonding involves shared valence electron density. Metals are often described using electrons delocalised across many atoms.
detail: Electronegativity difference helps interpret bond polarity, but bonding lies on a continuum. A molecule’s overall polarity depends on bond dipoles and three-dimensional shape. Ionic solids are extended lattices rather than collections of discrete salt molecules; a formula such as NaCl gives the simplest ionic ratio.
example: O–H bonds in water are polar covalent. Their dipoles do not cancel in water’s bent structure, so water is polar. The two C=O dipoles cancel in linear CO₂ even though each bond is polar.
question: What type of bonds occur within a water molecule?
explanation: Hydrogen and oxygen share electron pairs.
summary: Distinguish the type of bonding from a molecule’s overall polarity; shape matters as well as the individual bonds.
objectives: Distinguish ionic and covalent bonding
Relate molecular shape to molecular polarity

questions.question: What type of bonds occur within a water molecule?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen and oxygen share electron pairs.

questions.question: Why is linear CO₂ nonpolar overall?
options: Its C=O bonds are completely nonpolar
questions.explanation: The bonds are polar, but equal opposite dipoles give a zero net dipole.

questions.question: What does NaCl describe in a salt crystal?
questions.explanation: The formula gives the 1:1 ratio of Na⁺ to Cl⁻ in the ionic lattice.

title: The mole and chemical calculations
intro: The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076×10²³ specified entities. Molar mass links mass to amount of substance.
detail: Use n=m/M with n in mol, m in g and M in g/mol. State the entity being counted: atoms, molecules, ions or formula units. Coefficients in a balanced equation give mole ratios, not mass ratios. Keep units through the calculation and round the final result to the precision justified by the data.
example: With the approximate molar mass of water 18 g/mol, 36 g represents 36/18=2 mol. This corresponds to about 1.20×10²⁴ water molecules, not that number of hydrogen atoms: there are two H atoms in each molecule.
question: How many moles are in 36 g of water using a molar mass of approximately 18 g/mol?
explanation: Using approximately 18 g/mol: 36/18=2 mol.
summary: Convert mass to moles before using a reaction ratio, and identify exactly which entities are counted.
objectives: Convert between mass and amount of substance
Distinguish molecule counts from atom counts

questions.question: How many moles are in 36 g of water using a molar mass of approximately 18 g/mol?
questions.explanation: Using approximately 18 g/mol: 36/18=2 mol.

questions.question: How many moles of H atoms are in 2 mol of H₂O?
questions.explanation: Each water molecule has two H atoms: 2×2=4 mol of H atoms.

questions.question: Which molar mass unit is appropriate when mass is in grams?
questions.explanation: Dividing g by g/mol gives mol, consistent with n=m/M.

title: Solutions and dilution
intro: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent. Molarity is moles of solute per litre of final solution, not per litre of solvent alone.
detail: For an ideal dilution with no solute loss or reaction, C₁V₁=C₂V₂. Use the same volume unit on both sides, and distinguish final solution volume from solvent added. Dilution increases solution volume and decreases concentration while preserving solute amount. The relation does not describe solubility limits or chemical reactions.
example: Diluting 100 mL of a 1 M solution to a final volume of 500 mL gives C₂=1×100/500=0.2 M. Both solutions contain 0.1 mol of solute. The calculation uses final volume; it does not assume that mixing all liquids gives exactly additive volumes.
question: What is the final concentration when 100 mL of 1 M solution is diluted to 500 mL final volume without loss or reaction?
summary: Dilution conserves dissolved solute in this model. Specify final volume, units and the assumption of no reaction or loss.
objectives: Calculate a final concentration using solute conservation
Distinguish final solution volume from solvent added

questions.question: What is the final concentration when 100 mL of 1 M solution is diluted to 500 mL final volume without loss or reaction?
What stays constant during an ideal dilution?
questions.explanation: Adding solvent without loss or reaction preserves the amount of solute.

questions.question: In C₁V₁=C₂V₂, what does V₂ represent?
questions.explanation: V₂ is the total final solution volume after dilution.

title: Acids and bases
intro: In the Brønsted–Lowry model, an acid donates a proton and a base accepts one. pH expresses hydrogen ion activity on a logarithmic scale; concentration is a useful approximation in sufficiently dilute solutions.
detail: A conjugate acid–base pair differs by one proton. At 25 °C neutral pure water is near pH 7 because the water ionisation product is approximately 10⁻¹⁴. Neutrality means equal hydrogen and hydroxide activities, so neutral pH changes with temperature. Acid strength describes ionisation tendency; it is different from concentration.
example: A dilute ideal solution with [H₃O⁺]=10⁻³ mol/L has pH≈3. A second solution at pH 4 has about one tenth that hydrogen ion concentration under the same approximation. A buffer resists small pH changes but has finite capacity.
question: Which statement is more accurate?
options: Any solution at pH 7 is neutral at every temperature
explanation: The water ionisation constant changes with temperature, so neutral pH changes.
summary: Treat pH as logarithmic and temperature dependent. Distinguish a strong acid from a concentrated acid, and a buffer from unlimited protection against change.
objectives: Calculate pH in a dilute ideal approximation
Distinguish acid strength from concentration

questions.question: Which statement is more accurate?
options: Any solution at pH 7 is neutral at every temperature
questions.explanation: The water ionisation constant changes with temperature, so neutral pH changes.

questions.question: If pH rises from 3 to 4 in the dilute approximation, how does [H₃O⁺] change?
questions.explanation: pH≈−log₁₀[H₃O⁺]; a one-unit rise corresponds to a tenfold decrease.

questions.question: Which pair differs by one proton?
options: An acid and its conjugate base
questions.explanation: Losing one proton converts an acid into its conjugate base.

title: Chemical equilibrium
intro: A reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium when forward and reverse rates are equal. Reactant and product concentrations need not be equal; microscopic reactions continue.
detail: The equilibrium constant K describes an activity ratio at a specified temperature. For aA+bB⇌cC+dD, K=a(C)ᶜa(D)ᵈ/[a(A)ᵃa(B)ᵇ]. Pure solids and liquids have unit activity in the usual expression. The reaction quotient Q has the same form at any state. Compare Q with K to predict net direction; a catalyst changes the approach rate but not K.
example: If K=10 and Q=2, net reaction forms products until Q approaches 10. If Q=20 the net direction is toward reactants. K alone does not say how quickly either change occurs.
question: If Q is less than K, what is the net reaction direction?
explanation: Products form, increasing Q toward K.
summary: Equilibrium concerns equal rates, not equal concentrations. Temperature fixes K; comparison of Q and K predicts the net direction.
objectives: Distinguish Q from K
Explain how a catalyst affects equilibrium

questions.question: If Q is less than K, what is the net reaction direction?
questions.explanation: Products form, increasing Q toward K.

questions.question: If Q=20 and K=10, what is the net direction?
questions.explanation: Q must decrease to reach K, so net reaction forms reactants.

questions.question: What does a catalyst do at fixed temperature?
options: Speeds approach to equilibrium without changing K
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers barriers for both directions without changing the free energy difference between states.

title: Introduction to instrumental analysis
intro: Instrumental analysis uses optical, electrical and separation measurements to identify substances or determine concentrations. A raw reading is not a validated result without calibration, blanks and quality control.
detail: Method validation considers selectivity, range, precision, bias, detection and quantification limits, and measurement uncertainty. The relevant matrix and intended use determine what performance is needed. Repeatability describes agreement among repeats; agreement does not prove closeness to the true value. A calibration curve must not be extrapolated beyond its validated range without justification.
example: Three readings of 9.9, 10.0 and 10.1 mg/L cluster closely, but all may be biased if a certified control is 12.0 mg/L. A blank assesses background or contamination; a control material with an assigned value checks performance independently.
question: What is the purpose of a blank?
explanation: A blank helps assess background and contamination.
summary: Interpret a number together with units, matrix, method range, quality controls and uncertainty. Precision and trueness are different properties.
objectives: Distinguish repeatability from bias
Explain the roles of blanks and control materials

questions.question: What is the purpose of a blank?
questions.explanation: A blank helps assess background and contamination.

questions.question: Closely clustered results far from a reference value indicate what?
questions.explanation: Repeatability describes agreement among results; systematic bias can still displace them from the reference.

questions.question: What should happen when a signal exceeds the validated calibration range?
options: Follow a validated laboratory method to bring it into range
questions.explanation: Unvalidated extrapolation is unreliable; an approved procedure and appropriate remeasurement are needed.

title: Mineralogy and gold ores
intro: Ore characterisation examines mineral phases, grain textures and elemental distribution. Gold can occur as visible grains, microscopic particles or associated with other mineral phases; its appearance alone is not a reliable assay.
detail: XRF assesses elemental composition, XRD identifies crystalline phases, and microscopy examines texture. These tools answer different questions and have matrix effects and detection limits. Sampling must represent the material: a rich isolated grain is not an average grade. Contained metal is a mass balance, while an ore designation additionally requires economic and technical assessment.
example: A hypothetical 100 kg sample at 5 g/t contains 0.1 t×5 g/t=0.5 g of gold. This is theoretical contained metal before losses, not a recovery guarantee or extraction procedure. A separate mineralogical assessment is needed to understand the host phases.
question: What is the theoretical gold content of 100 kg of material at a grade of 5 g/t?
explanation: 100 kg=0.1 metric tonne, and 0.1×5=0.5 g.
summary: Link a grade to a representative sample, analytical method and uncertainty. Elemental composition, mineral identity and economic viability are separate questions.
objectives: Calculate theoretical contained metal from mass and grade
Distinguish elemental analysis from mineral phase identification

questions.question: What is the theoretical gold content of 100 kg of material at a grade of 5 g/t?
questions.explanation: 100 kg=0.1 metric tonne, and 0.1×5=0.5 g.

questions.question: Which technique primarily identifies crystalline phases?
questions.explanation: X-ray diffraction distinguishes crystal structures; elemental analysis alone does not identify the phase.

questions.question: Does one gold grain establish an area’s average grade?
questions.explanation: Spatial representation and grade variability matter; a selected grain may not represent the bulk.

title: Organic chemistry
intro: Organic chemistry examines the structures, properties and transformations of carbon compounds. Carbon can form chains, branches and rings, while heteroatoms such as oxygen and nitrogen create many functional groups.
detail: A molecular formula gives atom counts; a structural formula gives connections. Four bonds around neutral carbon is a useful starting rule for common molecules, but charge and bonding must also be checked. Functional groups explain characteristic patterns without determining every property: chain length, shape and the surrounding groups also matter.
example: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, is an alcohol. Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, contains a carboxyl group. Both contain O–H, but the adjacent carbonyl makes the acid chemically different; identifying one atom group in isolation can misclassify the compound.
question: Which group identifies a carboxylic acid?
explanation: A carboxyl group combines a carbonyl and hydroxyl on the same carbon: COOH.
summary: Read atom connectivity as well as formula. A carboxyl group is COOH; an alcohol hydroxyl is attached to saturated carbon.
objectives: Distinguish molecular and structural formulae
Identify the carboxyl group

questions.question: Which group identifies a carboxylic acid?
questions.explanation: A carboxyl group combines a carbonyl and hydroxyl on the same carbon: COOH.

questions.question: What does a structural formula add to atom counts?
questions.explanation: A molecular formula supplies counts; a structural formula shows bonding and connectivity.

questions.question: Which statement about a functional group is more accurate?
options: It explains patterns, with the rest of the structure also important
It determines every property without exception
questions.explanation: Functional groups matter greatly, but chain length, shape and structural context also matter.

title: Thermodynamics
intro: Thermodynamics studies energy transfer and the constraints on chemical and physical changes. The system is the chosen material under study; everything else is its surroundings.
detail: The first law expresses energy conservation: ΔU=q+w with heat entering the system and work done on it counted positive. At constant pressure and with only pressure–volume work, heat equals ΔH. Negative ΔH means exothermic change. Spontaneity at fixed temperature and pressure depends on ΔG=ΔH−TΔS, not enthalpy alone; a favourable process can still be slow.
example: If ΔH=−20 kJ, the stated process releases 20 kJ at constant pressure under the usual assumptions. If ΔH=10 kJ and TΔS=15 kJ, ΔG=−5 kJ; an endothermic change can therefore be thermodynamically favourable.
question: What does a negative ΔH indicate?
explanation: Under constant-pressure conditions with only pressure–volume work, a negative ΔH means heat leaves the system.
summary: Energy is conserved; heat depends on process conditions. Enthalpy, spontaneity and reaction rate answer different questions.
objectives: Interpret the sign of an enthalpy change
Calculate ΔG using consistent units

questions.question: What does a negative ΔH indicate?
questions.explanation: Under constant-pressure conditions with only pressure–volume work, a negative ΔH means heat leaves the system.

questions.question: If ΔH=10 kJ and TΔS=15 kJ, what is ΔG?
questions.explanation: ΔG=ΔH−TΔS=10−15=−5 kJ.

questions.question: Does a negative ΔG guarantee a fast reaction?
options: No; rate depends on the activation barrier
questions.explanation: Thermodynamics addresses favourability; kinetics addresses the rate of approach.

title: Chemical kinetics
intro: Chemical kinetics studies how fast reactions occur and how rate depends on concentration, temperature and reaction pathways. Rate is distinct from the final equilibrium composition.
detail: A rate law such as rate=k[A]² is determined experimentally, not read directly from the overall balanced equation unless a justified elementary step is involved. Increasing temperature often increases the fraction of collisions able to cross an activation barrier. A catalyst provides another pathway with lower barriers for both directions and does not change the equilibrium constant.
example: For rate=k[A]² at fixed temperature, doubling [A] makes the rate four times larger. A process may be favourable thermodynamically but take a long time because its activation barrier is large.
question: What does kinetics study?
explanation: Kinetics examines rates and pathways rather than only the final extent of change.
summary: Determine reaction orders from evidence, distinguish rate from equilibrium, and interpret catalysis as a pathway change.
objectives: Calculate a concentration effect from a given rate law
Distinguish kinetics from equilibrium

questions.question: What does kinetics study?
questions.explanation: Kinetics examines rates and pathways rather than only the final extent of change.

questions.question: For rate=k[A]², what does doubling [A] do at fixed k?
questions.explanation: (2[A])²=4[A]², so the rate increases fourfold.

questions.question: How are rate-law orders for an overall reaction usually found?
questions.explanation: An overall equation does not establish the mechanism; orders are measured experimentally.

title: Spectroscopic analysis
intro: Spectroscopy studies interactions between electromagnetic radiation and matter. Absorption, emission and scattering reveal different kinds of information about atoms and molecules.
detail: Atomic spectra reflect transitions between electronic energy levels. Molecular spectra can also probe vibration and rotation. Quantitative interpretation requires suitable calibration, background correction, control of interferences and an established working range. A method’s detection limit belongs to a defined procedure and matrix; a signal below it does not establish zero concentration.
example: If a validated method reports a sample below a detection limit of 0.02 mg/L, the appropriate conclusion is that it was not detected by that method at that limit. Reporting exactly 0 mg/L would discard the method’s limitation.
question: Does a result below the detection limit prove complete absence?
options: Yes; every instrument detects any amount
No; non-detection is limited by the method
It means concentration exactly equals the detection limit
explanation: A measurement below the detection limit does not establish a zero concentration.
summary: Match the spectroscopic method to the question. Report units, interferences and detection limits together with the result.
objectives: Distinguish absorption from emission
Interpret a result below the detection limit

questions.question: Does a result below the detection limit prove complete absence?
options: Yes; every instrument detects any amount
No; non-detection is limited by the method
It means concentration exactly equals the detection limit
questions.explanation: A measurement below the detection limit does not establish a zero concentration.

questions.question: What does a result below a 0.02 mg/L detection limit mean?
options: The method did not detect it at that limit
questions.explanation: Non-detection is conditional on method sensitivity and measurement conditions, not proof of absolute absence.

questions.question: What causes atomic spectral lines?
questions.explanation: An atom absorbs or emits a defined energy when its electronic state changes.

title: Mineralogy
intro: A mineral is generally a naturally occurring solid with an ordered internal structure and a characteristic chemical composition that may vary within defined limits. A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals.
detail: Hardness, streak, density, cleavage and crystal form are complementary observations. Hardness is resistance to scratching, not resistance to breaking. Colour may vary with impurities, and different minerals can share a colour. Definitive identification may require diffraction, microscopy or chemical analysis; visual identification is provisional.
example: Pyrite, FeS₂, can have a gold-like colour but is not native gold. Diamond and graphite are both carbon minerals yet have very different properties because their bonding and crystal structures differ.
question: Does a gold colour alone establish the presence of gold?
options: Yes; colour alone identifies the element
No; it may be another mineral such as pyrite
It establishes gold purity but not quantity
explanation: Hardness, structure and appropriate analysis distinguish minerals; colour alone is insufficient.
summary: Use several properties and the crystal structure to identify minerals. Appearance alone does not establish identity or economic value.
objectives: Distinguish a mineral from a rock
Explain property differences in materials with the same elemental composition

questions.question: Does a gold colour alone establish the presence of gold?
options: Yes; colour alone identifies the element
No; it may be another mineral such as pyrite
It establishes gold purity but not quantity
questions.explanation: Hardness, structure and appropriate analysis distinguish minerals; colour alone is insufficient.

questions.question: What does hardness measure?
options: Resistance to every kind of fracture
questions.explanation: Hardness describes scratching resistance; toughness and fracture behaviour are different properties.

questions.question: Why do diamond and graphite differ even though both are carbon?
questions.explanation: Crystal arrangement and bonding strongly influence properties.

title: Chemical safety
intro: Chemical safety starts with identifying hazards and evaluating possible exposure. Hazard is the potential to cause harm; risk also depends on exposure, task conditions and controls.
detail: The hierarchy of controls prioritises elimination and substitution, followed by engineering controls, administrative controls and personal protective equipment. An SDS describes hazards, first aid, storage and exposure controls, but must be applied by trained staff to the specific task. A pictogram signals a hazard category rather than a complete operating instruction.
example: If a toxic release is suspected, move away from the affected area, warn others without entering danger and call the local emergency service or trained response team. Do not attempt an untrained rescue or improvise chemical treatment. The correct emergency contact is set locally.
question: What is the priority during a toxic release?
explanation: Move away and call trained responders; personal protective equipment alone does not guarantee safety.
summary: Prevent exposure before relying on personal protective equipment. Use current SDS information and a site-specific trained emergency plan.
objectives: Distinguish hazard from risk
Order the hierarchy of controls

questions.question: What is the priority during a toxic release?
questions.explanation: Move away and call trained responders; personal protective equipment alone does not guarantee safety.

questions.question: Which control has highest priority in the hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Elimination removes the hazard; personal protective equipment is lower in the hierarchy.

questions.question: Does a hazard pictogram replace an SDS and task assessment?
questions.explanation: A pictogram summarises a hazard class; detailed information and task-specific controls remain necessary.

title: Measurement and units
intro: A measurement states a quantity with a unit and a limit to its certainty. Accuracy concerns closeness to a reference; precision concerns agreement among repeated measurements.
detail: Unit conversion multiplies by ratios equal to one. Density is mass divided by volume. Significant figures communicate measurement precision, but do not replace an uncertainty estimate. In multiplication or division the least precise input limits the reported precision; keep extra digits during calculation and round once at the end.
example: A sample with mass 24 g and volume 8.0 cm³ has density 24/8.0=3.0 g/cm³. Also 250 mL×(1 L/1000 mL)=0.250 L; units cancel explicitly. If the volume were written merely 8 cm³, a two-figure result would not be justified by that notation.
question: What is the density of a sample with mass 24 g and volume 8 cm³?
explanation: Density=mass/volume=24/8=3 g/cm³; the reported precision depends on the input precision.
summary: Carry units through every step, distinguish accuracy from precision, and report only the precision supported by the inputs.
objectives: Convert volume using a correct conversion factor
Calculate density with units

questions.question: What is the density of a sample with mass 24 g and volume 8 cm³?
questions.explanation: Density=mass/volume=24/8=3 g/cm³; the reported precision depends on the input precision.

questions.question: How many litres equal 250 mL?
What does precision describe?
questions.explanation: Repeated values can cluster despite bias; precision is not the same as accuracy.

title: Isotopes and atomic mass
intro: Isotopes of an element have the same proton count but different neutron counts. Their chemical behaviour is often similar, while their masses and nuclear stability can differ.
detail: Average atomic mass is a weighted average of isotope masses using their abundances. Fractions must add to one. Mass number is an integer count for a particular isotope, whereas isotope mass and average atomic mass are measured quantities and need not be integers. Some elements have no stable isotopes, so a bracketed mass number is commonly used instead of a standard atomic weight.
example: For hypothetical isotopes with masses 10 u and 11 u at 20% and 80%, average mass=(10×0.20)+(11×0.80)=10.8 u. This does not mean that an individual atom has mass number 10.8.
question: What is the same in isotopes of an element?
explanation: Isotopes share the proton count that identifies the element, while their neutron counts differ.
summary: Separate isotope mass, mass number and weighted atomic mass. An average does not describe an individual atom.
objectives: Calculate a weighted atomic mass from abundance
Distinguish mass number from average atomic mass

questions.question: What is the same in isotopes of an element?
questions.explanation: Isotopes share the proton count that identifies the element, while their neutron counts differ.

questions.question: What is the average of masses 10 and 11 at 20% and 80%?
Does an average of 10.8 mean an atom has mass number 10.8?
options: No; mass number is an integer count
questions.explanation: The weighted average describes a population; mass number counts protons and neutrons in one atom.

title: Balancing chemical equations
intro: A chemical equation represents changes of substances while conserving atoms of each element. A balanced equation must also conserve net electric charge when ions are involved.
detail: Change coefficients in front of formulae, never subscripts inside a formula. Use the smallest whole-number ratio conventionally. Coefficients give relative numbers of particles or moles; they do not establish a reaction mechanism or equal mass ratios. Count each element independently on both sides as a final check.
example: The digital model 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O has four H atoms and two O atoms on each side. Writing H₂O₂ instead of H₂O would change the product identity rather than balance water formation. This is a numerical model, not an instruction to perform the reaction.
question: What may be changed when balancing an equation?
explanation: Change coefficients to conserve atoms without changing the identities of the substances.
summary: Balance atoms and charge using coefficients. Preserve chemical identities and distinguish mole ratios from mass ratios.
objectives: Check atom conservation in an equation
Distinguish coefficients from subscripts

questions.question: What may be changed when balancing an equation?
questions.explanation: Change coefficients to conserve atoms without changing the identities of the substances.

questions.question: How many H atoms are represented by 2H₂O?
questions.explanation: The coefficient 2 multiplies two H atoms per water molecule, giving 4.

questions.question: What happens if H₂O is changed to H₂O₂ while balancing?
questions.explanation: A subscript is part of a compound’s identity; changing it gives another compound.

title: The limiting reactant
intro: The limiting reactant runs out first according to the stoichiometric proportions and sets the theoretical maximum product. An excess reactant remains after this idealised complete reaction.
detail: Compare each available amount in moles divided by its coefficient. The smallest ratio gives the theoretical reaction extent; multiply that extent by a product coefficient to obtain its amount. Actual yield can be smaller because of incomplete reaction, side reactions or losses. Percent yield is actual/theoretical×100 and does not identify the limiting reactant by itself.
example: For A+2B→C with 3 mol A and 4 mol B, the ratios are 3/1=3 and 4/2=2. B limits the extent to 2 mol. This yields at most 2 mol C and leaves 1 mol A. If 1.5 mol C is obtained, yield is 75%.
question: For A+2B→C with 3 mol A and 4 mol B, which is the limiting reactant?
explanation: Available moles divided by coefficients are 3 for A and 2 for B, so B limits the reaction.
summary: Use mole-to-coefficient ratios before deciding what runs out. Keep theoretical product, excess reactant and actual yield separate.
objectives: Identify a limiting reactant using mole ratios
Calculate excess reactant and yield

questions.question: For A+2B→C with 3 mol A and 4 mol B, which is the limiting reactant?
questions.explanation: Available moles divided by coefficients are 3 for A and 2 for B, so B limits the reaction.

questions.question: How much A remains in the example?
questions.explanation: Forming 2 mol C consumes 2 mol A, leaving 3−2=1 mol.

questions.question: If theoretical yield is 2 mol and actual yield is 1.5 mol, what is percent yield?
questions.explanation: Percent yield=1.5/2×100=75%.

title: Ideal gases
intro: The ideal gas model relates pressure, volume, absolute temperature and amount of gas. It treats particles as having negligible volume and negligible intermolecular interactions except during collisions.
detail: Use PV=nRT with temperature in kelvin and units consistent with R. Absolute pressure is required. At fixed n and T, pressure is inversely proportional to volume; at fixed n and P, volume is proportional to T. Real gases deviate more strongly at high pressure and low temperature, especially near condensation.
example: At fixed n and T, doubling volume halves pressure. A gas initially at 300 K heated to 600 K at constant volume and amount doubles its pressure. Heating from 20 °C to 40 °C does not double absolute temperature because these are 293.15 K and 313.15 K.
question: What happens to an ideal gas pressure when its volume doubles at fixed temperature and amount?
explanation: At fixed amount and temperature, PV is constant, so doubling volume halves pressure.
summary: Use kelvin, absolute pressure and consistent units. State which variables are held fixed before applying a proportionality.
objectives: Apply pressure–volume proportionality with its conditions
Convert Celsius temperature to kelvin

questions.question: What happens to an ideal gas pressure when its volume doubles at fixed temperature and amount?
questions.explanation: At fixed amount and temperature, PV is constant, so doubling volume halves pressure.

questions.question: Which temperature scale belongs in PV=nRT?
questions.explanation: The law requires absolute temperature in kelvin.

questions.question: At fixed volume and n, raising T from 300 K to 600 K does what to pressure?
questions.explanation: P=nRT/V makes pressure directly proportional to T under these conditions.

title: Molecular geometry
intro: Regions of electron density around a central atom determine electron-domain geometry; molecular shape describes the positions of atoms only. Prediction begins with a Lewis structure and a count of bonds and lone pairs.
detail: In VSEPR, electron domains separate to reduce repulsion. A single, double, or triple bond counts as one domain. Two domains give a linear arrangement, three a trigonal planar arrangement, and four a tetrahedral arrangement. Lone pairs occupy space and affect bond angles, so water has different domain geometry and molecular shape. The model is qualitative and does not describe every metal complex.
example: CH₄ has four bonds and no lone pairs on carbon: it is tetrahedral, with angles near 109.5°. H₂O has four domains around oxygen, including two lone pairs; its shape is bent and its angle is about 104.5°.
summary: Count domains first, then omit lone pairs when naming molecular shape. Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.
objectives: Count electron domains from a Lewis structure.
Distinguish a bent shape from tetrahedral domain geometry.
question: What is the shape of methane?
explanation: Four bonding domains and no lone pairs around carbon give a tetrahedral shape.

questions.question: What is the shape of methane?
questions.explanation: Four bonding domains and no lone pairs around carbon give a tetrahedral shape.

questions.question: How many VSEPR domains does a double bond represent?
questions.explanation: Each bond between two atoms counts as one domain, regardless of bond order.

questions.question: Why is the molecular shape of water not called tetrahedral?
options: Shape names count atom positions, excluding lone pairs
questions.explanation: Oxygen has four domains, but the two hydrogen positions define a bent molecular shape.

title: Intermolecular forces
intro: Intermolecular forces attract separate molecules and differ from bonds within a molecule. They help explain boiling, condensation, and solution properties.
detail: London dispersion forces occur in all atoms and molecules and generally increase with polarizability and contact area. Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules. Hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F can form hydrogen bonds with suitable lone pairs. Boiling generally separates molecules rather than breaking their internal covalent bonds. Molecular shape, mass, and structure must be considered together.
example: Water forms hydrogen bonds between molecules; each O–H bond within a molecule is covalent. When water boils, most particles remain H₂O rather than becoming hydrogen and oxygen.
summary: Distinguish internal bonds from attractions between molecules. Neither mass alone nor hydrogen bonding alone predicts every boiling point.
objectives: Classify dispersion, dipole–dipole, and hydrogen-bonding interactions.
Explain why boiling is usually a physical change.
question: Which interaction is prominent between water molecules?
explanation: Water has O–H groups and lone pairs that support intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

questions.question: Which interaction is prominent between water molecules?
questions.explanation: Water has O–H groups and lone pairs that support intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

questions.question: Where do London dispersion forces occur?
questions.explanation: Fluctuating electron distributions generate dispersion even in nonpolar particles.

questions.question: What usually happens when pure water boils?
options: The atomic number of oxygen changes
questions.explanation: Intermolecular attractions are overcome without changing the chemical identity of water.

title: Oxidation and reduction
intro: Oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain. They occur together because electrons lost by one species are gained by another in the overall reaction.
detail: An oxidation state is a bookkeeping quantity and is not always an actual atomic charge. It increases on oxidation and decreases on reduction. The oxidizing agent accepts electrons and is reduced; the reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidized. Oxidation states sum to the species charge, and a free element has oxidation state zero. Redox equations conserve both atoms and charge.
example: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ is oxidation because the oxidation state rises from +2 to +3. In Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, copper is reduced and Cu²⁺ acts as an oxidizing agent. These are electron-bookkeeping examples.
summary: Track electron transfer or oxidation-state changes, and identify the oxidizing agent as the species reduced. Conserve charge as well as atoms.
objectives: Identify oxidation and reduction from a half-equation.
Distinguish oxidizing and reducing agents.
question: Is losing an electron oxidation or reduction?
explanation: Loss of electrons raises the oxidation state and is oxidation.

questions.question: Is losing an electron oxidation or reduction?
questions.explanation: Loss of electrons raises the oxidation state and is oxidation.

questions.question: What happens to an oxidizing agent?
options: It is reduced by gaining electrons
It never changes in a reaction
questions.explanation: An oxidizing agent oxidizes another species while accepting electrons itself.

questions.question: What is the oxidation state of oxygen in free O₂?
questions.explanation: Every element in its elemental form has oxidation state zero.

title: Electrochemical cells
intro: A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous chemical reaction into electrical energy. Separating the half-reactions provides an electron path and an ion path to complete the circuit.
detail: Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode in both galvanic and electrolytic cells. In a galvanic cell electrons travel externally from anode to cathode, while a salt bridge transports ions to maintain electrical neutrality. Using reduction potentials, E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. Free energy is related by ΔG° = −nFE°. Actual voltage depends on activities and temperature; do not multiply potentials by equation coefficients.
example: If the standard reduction potential is 0.80 V at the cathode and 0.20 V at the anode, E°cell = 0.60 V. The positive sign corresponds to negative ΔG° for the written reaction under standard conditions.
summary: Remember oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Distinguish electron transport in a wire from ion transport in solution.
objectives: Calculate cell voltage from two reduction potentials.
Explain the function of a salt bridge.
question: Where does reduction occur?
explanation: Reduction always occurs at the cathode.

questions.question: Where does reduction occur?
questions.explanation: Reduction always occurs at the cathode.

questions.question: What is the cell voltage for the 0.80 and 0.20 V reduction potentials in the example?
questions.explanation: Subtract the anode reduction potential from the cathode reduction potential.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a salt bridge?
options: Transport ions to maintain electrical neutrality
questions.explanation: Electrons use the external circuit; the bridge allows ion transport.

title: Titration and curves
intro: Titration determines an unknown amount from a measured amount of standard reagent that reacts in a known stoichiometric ratio. A curve plots a response, such as pH, against added titrant volume.
detail: The equivalence point is the stoichiometric point; the endpoint is an observed signal, such as an indicator change. Their difference can introduce systematic error. For aA + bB, equivalence requires nA/a = nB/b. Standard concentration, units, blank correction, and volume uncertainty affect the result. Equivalence pH is not always 7; it depends on acid/base chemistry and temperature.
example: In a 1:1 calculation, 0.0020 mol of titrant corresponds to 0.0020 mol of analyte. If the analyte volume is 0.0200 L, its concentration is 0.10 mol/L. Convert mL to L when using n=CV. The result is rounded to two significant figures, limited by the amount of substance.
summary: Use the mole ratio before calculating concentration, and distinguish equivalence from endpoint. Do not assume every curve has an equivalence pH of 7.
objectives: Calculate a concentration from a 1:1 titration model.
Explain the difference between equivalence point and endpoint.
question: Does an observed titration end point always coincide with the stoichiometric equivalence point?
options: No; an experimental difference may occur
Equivalence is determined by solution colour alone
explanation: The endpoint is an observed signal and can differ from the exact stoichiometric point.

questions.question: Does an observed titration end point always coincide with the stoichiometric equivalence point?
options: No; an experimental difference may occur
Equivalence is determined by solution colour alone
questions.explanation: The endpoint is an observed signal and can differ from the exact stoichiometric point.

questions.question: What is the concentration of 0.0020 mol in 0.0200 L?
questions.explanation: C=n/V=0.0020/0.0200=0.10 mol/L. Report two significant figures.

questions.question: Is the equivalence pH 7 for every acid–base titration?
options: Only because solution volume is constant
No; it depends on the species and temperature
questions.explanation: Ions may hydrolyze at equivalence, producing an acidic or basic solution.

title: Chromatography
intro: Chromatography separates mixture components through their different interactions with a stationary phase and a mobile phase. The mobile phase may be a liquid or gas, depending on the technique.
detail: A component spending more time associated with the stationary phase generally moves more slowly. Column methods measure retention time; planar methods may use Rf, the component distance divided by solvent-front distance from the origin. Results depend on solvent, temperature, and phase type. Retention time alone does not prove identity: different substances can coelute. Peak area needs calibration before it represents an amount.
example: In a paper-chromatography model, a component moves 3 cm and the solvent front moves 6 cm from the origin: Rf=0.50. Two resolved peaks show two separable responses but do not prove that each peak contains only one substance.
summary: Separation reflects different distributions and interactions. Identification and quantification require standards and quality controls. Peak count is not always total component count.
objectives: Explain retention through interactions with the two phases.
Calculate Rf and state its identification limits.
question: What is the basis of chromatographic separation?
explanation: Components interact differently with stationary and mobile phases.

questions.question: What is the basis of chromatographic separation?
questions.explanation: Components interact differently with stationary and mobile phases.

questions.question: What is Rf when a component moves 3 cm and the solvent front 6 cm?
questions.explanation: Rf=3/6=0.50; it is dimensionless.

questions.question: Does one chromatographic peak guarantee a single substance?
options: Yes if the peak is tall
questions.explanation: Different components can produce overlapping responses under the chosen separation conditions.

title: Beer–Lambert law
intro: The Beer–Lambert law relates absorbance to absorbing-species concentration and path length under defined conditions. Absorbance does not represent every possible cause of reduced light intensity.
detail: A=εbc, where dimensionless A=−log₁₀(T), T=I/I₀, b is path length, and ε is molar absorptivity. With b in cm and c in mol/L, ε has units L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. The model assumes suitable radiation and a stable absorbing species. Scattering, stray light, and changing chemical equilibria can cause deviations. A blank corrects solvent and cell contributions; a calibration curve is used within its validated range.
example: For ε=100 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, b=1 cm, and c=0.002 mol/L, A=0.2. Doubling concentration within the linear range, with b and ε fixed, gives A=0.4.
summary: Record the units of ε, b, and c, and distinguish absorbance from transmittance. Linearity must be checked experimentally and does not justify unlimited extrapolation.
objectives: Calculate A from ε, b, and c with consistent units.
Identify a cause of nonlinearity.
question: What is absorbance A for ε=100 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, b=1 cm and c=0.002 mol/L within the Beer–Lambert law’s valid range?
explanation: A=100×1×0.002=0.2, which is dimensionless.

questions.question: What is absorbance A for ε=100 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, b=1 cm and c=0.002 mol/L within the Beer–Lambert law’s valid range?
questions.explanation: A=100×1×0.002=0.2, which is dimensionless.

questions.question: How does A change when concentration doubles within the linear range and all else stays fixed?
questions.explanation: A=εbc makes A directly proportional to c under the model conditions.

questions.question: Which effect can make reduced transmitted intensity misleading as pure absorption?
questions.explanation: Scattering removes light from the measured beam and can appear as apparent absorbance.

title: Hydrocarbons
intro: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Classifying their bonds and chain or ring structure helps explain their properties.
detail: Alkanes have single carbon–carbon bonds; open-chain saturated alkanes have formula CnH₂n+₂. Alkenes contain a double bond and alkynes a triple bond. An open-chain compound with one double bond has formula CnH₂n, but the formula alone cannot distinguish an alkene from a saturated ring. Aromaticity involves a conjugated electron system and structural conditions, not simply odor. Within a comparable series, boiling points generally rise with size, while branching also matters.
example: Ethane, C₂H₆, has a single C–C bond; ethene, C₂H₄, has a double bond. C₃H₆ can describe propene or cyclopropane, so a structural formula is needed to distinguish them.
summary: Classify from structure rather than molecular formula alone. A hydrocarbon contains no oxygen or nitrogen in its composition.
objectives: Distinguish alkanes, alkenes, and alkynes from their bonds.
Explain why CnH₂n alone does not prove a double bond.
question: Which compound contains a double bond?
explanation: Ethene is an alkene and contains a carbon–carbon double bond.

questions.question: Which compound contains a double bond?
questions.explanation: Ethene is an alkene and contains a carbon–carbon double bond.

questions.question: Which compound is a hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation: C₂H₆ contains only carbon and hydrogen; the other compounds contain oxygen.

questions.question: What is the general formula of an open-chain saturated alkane?
questions.explanation: A saturated acyclic carbon chain has formula CnH₂n+₂.

title: Functional groups
intro: A functional group is an arrangement of atoms and bonds that controls many reactions and properties of a compound. A molecule may contain more than one functional group.
detail: An alcohol has OH attached to saturated carbon; a phenol has OH attached to an aromatic ring. The C=O carbonyl occurs in aldehydes and ketones: the aldehyde carbon is bonded to hydrogen, whereas the ketone carbon is bonded to two carbon groups. A carboxylic acid contains COOH, and an ester has a –C(=O)–O– linkage with an organic group on the singly bonded oxygen. Functional groups influence polarity, hydrogen bonding, and acidity, but chain length and the rest of the structure also matter.
example: CH₃CH₂OH is ethanol, an alcohol, and CH₃COOH is ethanoic acid. The OH inside COOH does not make the acid simply an alcohol; the complete group determines its behavior.
summary: Read the complete connectivity when identifying groups. Not every OH is a separate alcohol group.
objectives: Recognize alcohol, carbonyl, and carboxyl groups.
Distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone by carbonyl connectivity.
question: Which group identifies a carboxylic acid?
explanation: The carboxyl group COOH characterizes carboxylic acids.

questions.question: Which group identifies a carboxylic acid?
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group COOH characterizes carboxylic acids.

questions.question: Which group is shared by aldehydes and ketones?
questions.explanation: Both contain C=O, but the groups attached to its carbon differ.

questions.question: Does OH within COOH necessarily make the compound an alcohol?
options: No; the whole group connectivity determines its classification
questions.explanation: The OH is part of a carboxyl group, whose behavior differs from that of a simple alcohol.

title: Isomerism
intro: Isomers have the same molecular formula but differ in atom connectivity or spatial arrangement. Matching formulas do not guarantee matching properties.
detail: Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity: chain structure, group position, or group identity may change. Stereoisomers retain connectivity but differ spatially; examples include geometric isomers with restricted rotation and nonsuperimposable mirror images. Not every mirror image is a distinct chiral form. Isomers may interact differently with biological systems, so structural characterization matters beyond molecular formula.
example: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, and dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃, both have formula C₂H₆O, but their connectivity and functional groups differ. They are constitutional isomers.
summary: Compare formula first, then connectivity, then spatial arrangement. The same formula does not establish the same toxicity or boiling point.
objectives: Classify a connectivity difference versus a spatial difference.
Explain why formula alone does not identify a compound.
question: What do ethanol and dimethyl ether share as isomers?
explanation: Both have formula C₂H₆O but different connectivity.

questions.question: What do ethanol and dimethyl ether share as isomers?
questions.explanation: Both have formula C₂H₆O but different connectivity.

questions.question: What differs between constitutional isomers?
options: The number of protons in carbon
questions.explanation: The formula stays the same while atom connectivity changes.

questions.question: What remains the same between stereoisomers?
questions.explanation: Spatial positions differ while the same pairs of atoms remain connected.

title: Polymers
intro: Polymers are large molecules with repeating structural units derived from smaller molecules called monomers. Polymers can be natural or synthetic.
detail: In addition polymerization, suitable monomer bonds are converted into bonds linking a chain; condensation polymerization may release small molecules. Molecular mass distribution, branching, crosslinking, and crystallinity influence properties. Thermoplastics may soften on heating, whereas thermoset networks do not melt in the same way. Recycling depends on polymer type, additives, contamination, and local collection infrastructure; a resin code alone does not establish actual recyclability.
example: Polyethylene contains repeated –CH₂–CH₂– units derived from ethene. The monomer is the ethene molecule before polymerization; the repeat unit is the segment within the linked chain.
summary: Distinguish a monomer from a repeat unit and relate properties to chain structure. No single recycling route applies to every polymer.
objectives: Identify the monomer and repeat unit in polyethylene.
Relate crosslinking and branching to broad polymer properties.
question: What is the small building-block molecule called?
explanation: A monomer is a small molecule from which polymer chains can be formed.

questions.question: What is the small building-block molecule called?
questions.explanation: A monomer is a small molecule from which polymer chains can be formed.

questions.question: Which monomer gives polyethylene?
questions.explanation: The ethene double bond is converted into links along the polyethylene chain.

questions.question: Does a resin code prove that plastic will be recycled locally?
options: No; it depends on local systems, material type, and condition
questions.explanation: The code identifies a material category but does not guarantee collection or processing.

title: Proteins and enzymes
intro: Proteins are amino-acid chains linked by peptide bonds. They perform structural, transport, and regulatory roles, and many enzymes are proteins.
detail: Primary structure is the amino-acid sequence; secondary structure is local organization; tertiary structure is overall folding; quaternary structure assembles multiple chains where present. Activity depends on active-site shape and environment. Enzymes lower activation barriers and accelerate approach to equilibrium in both directions without changing ΔG or the equilibrium constant. Temperature, pH, and inhibitors affect activity. Denaturation alters folding and may remove function without necessarily breaking peptide bonds.
example: If an enzyme shortens the time needed to reach equilibrium, the equilibrium composition remains the same at the same temperature. Denaturation can change the active-site shape and reduce substrate binding.
summary: Protein function depends on sequence, folding, and environment. Catalysis changes how fast equilibrium is reached, not where it lies.
objectives: Distinguish primary from tertiary protein structure.
Explain enzyme effects on activation energy and equilibrium.
question: Does an enzyme change the equilibrium constant?
explanation: Enzymes lower activation barriers without changing the equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature.

questions.question: Does an enzyme change the equilibrium constant?
questions.explanation: Enzymes lower activation barriers without changing the equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature.

questions.question: What defines primary protein structure?
questions.explanation: Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in the chain.

questions.question: What is the direct effect of enzyme catalysis?
questions.explanation: An enzyme provides a lower-barrier path without changing the free-energy difference between reactants and products.

title: Carbohydrates and lipids
intro: Carbohydrates and lipids are diverse classes of biological molecules. They contribute to energy storage, structure, cell recognition, and membranes.
detail: Monosaccharides such as glucose can join through glycosidic bonds into disaccharides and polysaccharides. Starch and cellulose are built from glucose, but different linkages change their properties and human digestibility. Lipids are not all polymers; they include triglycerides, phospholipids, and steroids. A phospholipid has hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions, which support membrane formation. Fatty-acid saturation and configuration affect packing.
example: Glucose is a monosaccharide and starch a polysaccharide. A triglyceride contains glycerol and three fatty-acid chains, while phospholipid structure supports organization into membrane layers.
summary: Properties depend on building blocks and linkages, not elemental composition alone. Distinguish energy storage by triglycerides from membrane roles of phospholipids.
objectives: Classify glucose and starch by carbohydrate size.
Explain the hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions of a phospholipid.
question: How is starch classified?
explanation: Starch is a polysaccharide built from many glucose units.

questions.question: How is starch classified?
questions.explanation: Starch is a polysaccharide built from many glucose units.

questions.question: Why do starch and cellulose differ despite both containing glucose units?
options: Their linkages and chain arrangements differ
Carbon has a different atomic number
questions.explanation: Different linkage patterns affect structure and enzyme interactions.

questions.question: Which property helps phospholipids form membranes?
options: They have both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions
questions.explanation: Their amphipathic nature directs their organization in water.

title: Coordination complexes
intro: A coordination complex has a central atom, often a metal, surrounded by ligands that donate electron pairs. Coordination chemistry explains the colors and properties of many compounds.
detail: Coordination number counts donor atoms directly bonded to the center, not necessarily ligand molecules. A multidentate ligand can bind through several donor atoms. Overall charge equals the metal oxidation state plus ligand charges. Geometry, d-electron count, and ligand identity affect energy splitting, color, and magnetism. Color alone does not establish complex identity or concentration without an appropriate analytical method.
example: In [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, six oxygen donor atoms come from six water molecules, giving coordination number 6. Water is neutral, so copper has oxidation state +2. Many six-coordinate complexes have octahedral arrangements, sometimes distorted.
summary: Count donor atoms and charge separately. Coordination number and oxidation state are different concepts.
objectives: Calculate coordination number from donor atoms.
Infer the metal oxidation state from complex charge.
question: What does coordination number count?
explanation: It counts donor atoms directly attached to the central atom.

questions.question: What does coordination number count?
questions.explanation: It counts donor atoms directly attached to the central atom.

questions.question: What is the copper coordination number in [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
questions.explanation: Six oxygen atoms are directly bonded to the copper center.

questions.question: What is the copper oxidation state in the same complex if water is neutral?
questions.explanation: Water contributes no charge, so the +2 complex charge equals the copper oxidation state.

title: Water chemistry
intro: Water-quality assessment requires chemical, physical, and microbial measurements linked to the intended use. Appearance and smell do not establish drinking-water safety.
detail: Conductivity responds to dissolved ions but does not identify them or detect every organic or microbial contaminant. Turbidity measures light scattering, pH describes acidity, and hardness mainly reflects calcium and magnesium. Each indicator has its own method, units, and interpretation limits. Sample representativeness, time, location, preservation, and chain of custody affect validity. Comparison needs an applicable standard for the intended use rather than a single limit for all waters.
example: Clear water with low turbidity can still contain invisible microbial contamination. High conductivity may indicate dissolved salts without showing whether they are chlorides, sulfates, or others; further qualitative and quantitative analysis is needed.
summary: Link each result to an indicator, method, unit, and intended use. Neither conductivity nor visual clarity provides a comprehensive safety certificate.
objectives: Distinguish conductivity, turbidity, and pH as different indicators.
Explain why microbial testing complements chemistry.
question: Does clear appearance alone establish drinking-water safety?
options: No; chemical or microbial contaminants may remain
Yes if it is also odourless
explanation: Invisible chemical or microbial contaminants may remain in clear water.

questions.question: Does clear appearance alone establish drinking-water safety?
options: No; chemical or microbial contaminants may remain
Yes if it is also odourless
questions.explanation: Invisible chemical or microbial contaminants may remain in clear water.

questions.question: What does conductivity alone establish?
options: An ion-related response without identifying the ions
questions.explanation: Multiple ionic species contribute; a single conductivity reading does not identify them.

questions.question: Why record sampling time and location?
options: To remove the need for an analytical method
To relate the result to sample representativeness
questions.explanation: Water quality can vary in space and time; a result applies to the documented sample.

title: Minerals and ores
intro: A mineral is a natural substance with a characteristic composition and crystal structure within defined ranges. An ore is material whose valuable constituent can be assessed for economic extraction under specific conditions; not every mineral is an ore.
detail: Hardness is resistance to scratching, streak is powder color, and cleavage is splitting along structural planes. These properties, density, and structure support initial identification, but similarity, weathering, and mixed phases may require mineralogical analysis. Grade, quantity, infrastructure, cost, and environmental requirements affect economic ore status. XRD identifies crystalline phases, whereas XRF provides elemental composition under method-specific limits; neither fully replaces the other.
example: Pyrite, FeS₂, and gold may look similar in color but differ in composition and structure. Quartz veins do not prove gold is present, and trace gold does not establish an economic ore.
summary: Mineral identification needs multiple lines of evidence, and economic assessment needs more than one sample. Distinguish an element, mineral, rock, and ore.
objectives: Distinguish mineral occurrence from an economic ore claim.
Compare the conceptual roles of XRD and XRF.
question: Does a rock’s gold-like lustre alone prove that it contains gold?
options: Yes; lustre is an elemental analysis
No; appropriate characterisation and analysis may be needed
Quartz makes such lustre conclusive evidence
explanation: Color and luster are insufficient; composition and mineralogical evidence are needed.

questions.question: Does a rock’s gold-like lustre alone prove that it contains gold?
options: Yes; lustre is an elemental analysis
No; appropriate characterisation and analysis may be needed
Quartz makes such lustre conclusive evidence
questions.explanation: Color and luster are insufficient; composition and mineralogical evidence are needed.

questions.question: Which technique targets crystalline-phase identification?
questions.explanation: X-ray diffraction depends on crystal arrangement and is used for phase identification.

questions.question: Does a trace concentration of an element make a rock an economic ore?
options: No; quantitative, economic, and environmental evidence is needed
questions.explanation: Chemical occurrence alone does not establish economic viability.

title: Gold analysis
intro: Gold grade in an ore differs from the fineness of a gold alloy. Grade describes element mass relative to sample mass; fineness describes its fraction in the alloy.
detail: g/t means grams per metric tonne of 1000 kg and is mass-ratio equivalent to mg/kg. Theoretical content equals mass in tonnes multiplied by grade in g/t. Assumed recovery is a separate arithmetic fraction, not a process guarantee or treatment method. Sampling matters because gold can be unevenly distributed in sparse grains. An accredited laboratory should report a matrix-suitable method, detection limits, uncertainty, and quality controls. One sample assay does not establish a reserve.
example: Hypothetical material of mass 2 t and grade 3 g/t contains a theoretical 6 g of gold. An arithmetic assumption of 80% recovery gives 4.8 g, but does not show that this can be achieved in practice.
summary: Check mass units and distinguish grade, fineness, and recovery. The calculator is an educational mass balance and needs representative data to be meaningful.
objectives: Calculate theoretical content from tonnes and g/t.
Explain the difference between grade, fineness, and recovery.
question: What is the theoretical gold content of 2 t of material at 3 g/t?
explanation: 2 t × 3 g/t = 6 g before any processing losses.

questions.question: What is the theoretical gold content of 2 t of material at 3 g/t?
questions.explanation: 2 t × 3 g/t = 6 g before any processing losses.

questions.question: Which mass ratio is equivalent to 1 g/t?
questions.explanation: 1 g per 1000 kg is 1000 mg per 1000 kg, or 1 mg/kg.

questions.question: What is 80% arithmetic recovery of a theoretical 6 g?
questions.explanation: 6×0.80=4.8 g; this is a calculation assumption, not an operating guarantee.

title: Yemen geology and sample documentation
intro: Claims of element occurrence require a geological source and a documented sample and location. Yemen includes old basement rocks, sedimentary cover, and volcanics; a regional label alone does not establish an ore deposit.
detail: Distinguish a geological indication, a geochemical anomaly, a resource, and an economic reserve. Record sample ID, coordinates and reference system, rock type, collection date, organization, analytical method, detection limits, and uncertainty, linked to an auditable report. Regional surveys do not automatically assign a grade to a particular district. Kaʿaydinah, Kushar, and Bani Qays in Hajjah remain areas requiring verification; this version contains no confirmed assays for them or validated deposit coordinates.
example: A national report mentioning gold is insufficient to assign it to a sample from Kushar. Auditable documentation links a site claim to sample ID, coordinates, laboratory method, and a primary source. Missing data leaves the claim unverified rather than proving absence of the element.
summary: Use national references for context and primary reports for specific locations. Local Hajjah data remain unverified here; no documented reserve estimates are supplied.
objectives: Identify the minimum documentation for a geological sample.
Distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence in a local claim.
question: If documented assays are unavailable for a site, does that establish that an element is absent?
options: It proves zero concentration throughout the site
No; occurrence or absence remains unverified
It establishes an economic ore deposit
explanation: Missing evidence leaves occurrence unverified; it does not establish absence.

questions.question: If documented assays are unavailable for a site, does that establish that an element is absent?
options: It proves zero concentration throughout the site
No; occurrence or absence remains unverified
It establishes an economic ore deposit
questions.explanation: Missing evidence leaves occurrence unverified; it does not establish absence.

questions.question: Does a national report alone assign a gold grade to a particular district?
options: No; local sample-linked documentation is needed
questions.explanation: The spatial scale matters; a general report does not establish a site-specific result.

questions.question: Which record makes an assay easier to audit?
options: Sample ID, coordinates, analytical method, and report source
questions.explanation: These data connect a result to a sample, location, and verifiable method.

title: Cyanide and lead hazards
intro: Cyanide can cause life-threatening acute poisoning, while lead is toxic and can cause cumulative harm. Monitoring pH alone does not eliminate cyanide hazards.
detail: Exposure can occur by inhalation, ingestion, or contact depending on chemical form. Lead can damage the nervous system, kidneys, and blood; children are especially vulnerable. Lead nitrate is an oxidizer and toxic, adding fire and lead-exposure hazards. If a release or exposure is suspected, leave the area, contact medical emergency services, and report the substance name if known from a safe location. Do not enter a contaminated area for rescue without specialist training and equipment, or attempt improvised neutralization or self-administered antidotes.
example: A worker has breathing difficulty near a toxic material: move to safety, keep others from entering, and contact emergency services. Trained responders assess and treat the exposure; do not wait for a pH reading before seeking help.
summary: Prevent further exposure and seek specialist response. This lesson provides no cyanide operating procedures, reagent doses, or treatment protocol.
objectives: Recognize acute cyanide hazards and cumulative lead toxicity.
Choose a safe initial response to suspected exposure.
question: What is the priority in the example?
explanation: Leave the hazardous area and seek trained emergency responders to avoid additional casualties.

questions.question: What is the priority in the example?
questions.explanation: Leave the hazardous area and seek trained emergency responders to avoid additional casualties.

questions.question: Does a reassuring pH reading prove that a cyanide-containing material is safe?
options: No; pH is not a comprehensive exposure assessment
Yes if there is no odor
questions.explanation: Toxicity, exposure routes, and other conditions still require specialist assessment.

questions.question: Why should an untrained person not enter a contaminated area to rescue someone?
options: They may be exposed and become another casualty
questions.explanation: Entry requires specialist assessment, equipment, and training; call responders from safety.

title: Respirable crystalline silica
intro: Silica risk comes from inhaling fine crystalline particles that can be generated while crushing, cutting, or grinding silica-containing materials. Visible dust does not directly measure respirable exposure.
detail: Exposure can cause silicosis, lung cancer, and chronic respiratory disease, and symptoms may be delayed. Occupational assessment considers tasks, exposure measurements, engineering controls, maintenance, training, and health surveillance under applicable standards. Elimination, substitution, and engineering controls take priority over relying solely on personal protective equipment. Respirator selection requires a professional program, fit assessment, and training; an unsuitable mask does not establish protection.
example: A worker with repeated dust exposure needs occupational assessment even without symptoms or a visible cloud. Safety decisions depend on measurements, task assessment, and controls rather than sight or how the worker feels alone.
summary: No symptoms or visible dust does not prove no exposure. Prevention is a specialist-assessed program rather than a mask alone.
objectives: Explain why exposure can matter before symptoms appear.
Place engineering controls and PPE in the hierarchy of controls.
question: Does absence of symptoms in a worker exposed to silica dust establish that exposure is safe?
options: Yes; silica harm always appears immediately
No; harm may be delayed and exposure needs assessment
Yes if the worker cannot see the dust
explanation: Silica-related disease can have delayed symptoms; exposure must be assessed.

questions.question: Does absence of symptoms in a worker exposed to silica dust establish that exposure is safe?
options: Yes; silica harm always appears immediately
No; harm may be delayed and exposure needs assessment
Yes if the worker cannot see the dust
questions.explanation: Silica-related disease can have delayed symptoms; exposure must be assessed.

questions.question: Which evidence is stronger than absence of visible dust for exposure assessment?
options: A feeling that the air is clean
questions.explanation: Hazardous particles may not be visible, so competent measurement and assessment are needed.

questions.question: Where does PPE sit in the hierarchy of controls?
options: It removes the need for training
Below higher-order controls such as elimination and engineering
questions.explanation: PPE relies on fit and correct use and complements other controls.

title: Permits and environmental assessment
intro: Permits and engineering and environmental review belong to the relevant authorities. Assessment identifies impacts, alternatives, and controls before activity decisions.
detail: Assessment considers water sources, communities, biodiversity, waste, occupational exposure, and emergencies, with baseline conditions, potential impacts, mitigation, monitoring, and closure. Responsibilities and stakeholder engagement should be documented and current local legal requirements verified. Environmental assessment does not replace a permit, and a permit does not remove ongoing compliance duties. The app is not an official approval, facility design, or complete legal checklist for Yemen.
example: A project without documented approvals requires review by competent authorities before activity begins. Completing an educational app form does not show that a permit has been issued or that a professional emergency plan is adequate.
summary: Link each obligation to an authority, current rule, and verifiable document. General references support understanding but do not replace local law.
objectives: Identify core components of environmental impact assessment.
Distinguish an educational checklist from a valid official approval.
question: Does completing an awareness checklist in the app constitute official activity authorisation?
options: Yes; it replaces the competent authority
No; official requirements and approvals must be checked
explanation: Only a competent authority can issue an applicable official approval.

questions.question: Does completing an awareness checklist in the app constitute official activity authorisation?
options: Yes; it replaces the competent authority
No; official requirements and approvals must be checked
questions.explanation: Only a competent authority can issue an applicable official approval.

questions.question: Which item belongs in environmental assessment?
options: Baseline conditions, monitoring, and closure planning
questions.explanation: Existing conditions, impact tracking, and the end of operations must be considered.

questions.question: Does a general international reference establish compliance with all current Yemeni laws?
options: Yes if it is in English
No; competent local legal verification is needed
questions.explanation: Laws, procedures, and authorities vary; educational guidance is not official approval.

title: Solubility and the solubility product
intro: Solubility describes how much of a substance can remain dissolved at a specified equilibrium with a solid phase. Dissolution rate differs from the solubility limit: stirring can speed the approach without necessarily increasing the limit.
detail: For hypothetical MX(s)⇌M⁺+X⁻, Ksp=a(M⁺)a(X⁻), approximated by the concentration product in a dilute ideal solution. If the salt is the only source of ions and other reactions are absent, molar solubility s gives Ksp≈s². An ion product Qsp greater than Ksp makes precipitation thermodynamically favourable, although nucleation depends on kinetics. Changes in pH or complex formation can change solubility.
example: For hypothetical MX with Ksp=10⁻⁸ in the dilute model, s=√10⁻⁸=10⁻⁴ mol/L. Do not apply s² to MX₂ without stoichiometry: if MX₂ dissolves alone, [M²⁺]=s and [X⁻]=2s, so Ksp≈4s³.
summary: Write the dissolution equilibrium and Ksp expression first. Distinguish dissolution rate from solubility equilibrium and state the approximation assumptions.
objectives: Write Ksp from a dissolution equation
